## Exploratory data analysis

The provided dataset consists of a four dimensional array comprised of 25 000 handwritten digits of 28 by 28 pixels and associated metadata. The five digits from 0 to 4 were each replicated 50 times by 20 different individuals during each of five independent sessions. The array contained no missing values, indicating all images were complete. Pixel values ranged from zero, indicating a blank background, to 255, representing a pixel completely covered in ink. 

Variation arose between individuals in several different ways (@fig-inter-ind_var). The size of digits written by different people varied and this was particularly pronounced in the digit zero. For example, individuals 3 and 12 had much smaller zeros than individuals 1, 10, and 16 (@fig-inter-ind_var). The angle of lines as well as the curve of the lines within the digits varied. The vertical line in digit one which was straight and vertical for individual 1, more curved for individual 3 and straight yet more diagonal for individual 10. The diagonal and vertical lines in digit four varied in angle and curvature across individuals, and the zeros tilted in different directions for individuals 10 and 12 compared to 1,3, and 16 (@fig-inter-ind_var). 

While inter-individual variation was more pronounced, there was still variation within individuals both across sessions (@fig-within-ind-var) and within a given session (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). The replicates of a digit for a given individual tended to be similar sized. Variation once again arose in the angle and curvature of certain lines such as the top right hand corner of the zeros which differed slightly and the angle of the horizontal line at the bottom of the digit two (@fig-within-ind-var). Intra-individual variation was more recognisable within an individual across different sessions than within an individual in the same session. For person 16, the line at the bottom of digit two was more a more similar angle across replicates in the same session than across different sessions. Across replicates from the same individual and the same session variability arose more in the density of the pixels which can be seen when looking at the bottom horizontal line of the digit one (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). 

There are some clearly visible limitations when using simulated data for handwritten digits. The first is the presence of unusually straight lines and sharp angles in digits where these are unlikely to occur. An example of this is in the top right corner of the digit zero for person 10 (@fig-inter-ind_var). The second is that in some digits the continuity of the line is interrupted, for example the gaps in the digit 2 in sessions 3,4 and 5 for person 16 (@fig-within-ind-var) and all the selected samples for digit two in session 1 (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). Further, the simulated handwritten data fails to mimic changes in the thickness of the font which is likely to occur in real world data where different people use variable pressure when writing. There is no variation in the style of digits. For example, the digit one can also be written as a single vertical line. In some cases, the simulation also does not look accurate, such as for person threes digit 1 which looks much more similar to a 2 and is unlikely to be written like this in real life.

```{.r .cell-code}
# Each fold needs a new model with fresh weights, so the model is built by a function
build_cnn <- function() {
  input <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

  # Ian's model structure taken from lecture slides
  output <- input %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3,3)) %>%
    layer_activation('relu') %>%
    layer_dropout(rate = 0.20) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3,3), activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(units = 20, activation = 'softmax')

  model <- keras_model(inputs = input, outputs = output)

  model %>% compile(
    loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.01),
    metrics = c('accuracy'),
  )

  model
}
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 5-fold cross-validation by session: train on four sessions, hold out the fifth
cnn_epochs <- 5
cnn_history <- list()
cnn_predictions <- list()

for (fold in 1:5) {
  train_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session != fold)
  test_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session == fold)

  x_train <- x[train_id,,,,drop = FALSE]
  y_train <- y[train_id,]
  x_test <- x[test_id,,,,drop = FALSE]
  y_test <- y[test_id,]

  set_random_seed(67)
  model <- build_cnn()

  history <- model %>% fit(
    x_train, y_train,
    epochs = cnn_epochs, batch_size = 8192,
    validation_data = list(x_test, y_test), shuffle = TRUE,
    verbose = 0
  )

  y_test_hat <- model %>% predict(x_test, verbose = 0) %>% op_argmax(axis = 2) %>% as.numeric()

  cnn_history[[fold]] <- tibble(fold = fold, epoch = 1:cnn_epochs,
                                train = history$metrics$accuracy,
                                held_out = history$metrics$val_accuracy)
  cnn_predictions[[fold]] <- as_tibble(handwriting$metadata[test_id,]) %>%
    mutate(fold = fold, predicted = y_test_hat)
}

# Save everything the rest of this section needs
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(summary = capture.output(print(build_cnn())), # untrained copy, so only the model's own parameters are counted
             history = bind_rows(cnn_history),
             predictions = bind_rows(cnn_predictions)),
        cnn_results_file)
```

## Writer verification with a Siamese network

<!-- Task 3: contrastive or triplet loss; how training examples are constructed; matching performance. -->
### Build a Siamese network that estimates whether two images were written by the same person. Use contrastive loss or triplet loss. Explain how you construct training examples and evaluate matching performance.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data <- readRDS("data/handwriting.rds")
#head(data$metadata)

library(keras3)
use_backend("tensorflow")

# images is an integer array with values from 0 (background) to 255 (ink).

# below = x in e.g.
x <- data$images / 255 # scale the pixels to 0-1
#dim(data$images) # 25000 x 28 x 28 x 1 - 1 = number of image channels (greyscale = 1)
# therefore: 25,000 images, 28 x 28 pixels, 1 image channel
#range(x) # 0 1

# below = 'labels' in e.g.
y_person <- data$metadata$person_id - 1L # subtracts 1 from every value in ID
#range(y_person) # 0 19 = 20 people

set.seed(25)
```
:::


We want to evaluate whether two images were written by the same writer. Therefore,
we must control for the digit identity i.e., construct pairs using the same digit
to force the NN to learn the writing style (the writer identity).
(Positive pair: same writer + same digit; Negative pair: diff writer + same digit).




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# need pairs of image indices to compare
# use person_id to decide if positive / negative pair

make_pairs <- function(ids, # indices of images it can use
                       n, # how many pairs to create
                       metadata){ # metadata -> writer ID + digit ID for each image
  
  # a: choose the first image in every pair - randomly selects n IDs
  a <- sample(ids, n, replace = TRUE) # w/replacement = can make as many pairs as we want
  
  # b: create the second image in every pair
  b <- vapply(a, function(i){
    
    # randomly decide if pair is from same writer or not
    same <- runif(1) < 0.5 
    
    # finds pool of images with the same digit
    pool <- ids[metadata$digit[ids] == metadata$digit[i]]
    
    if(same){ # if the same writer, pool must be same writer + same digit (pos pair)
      
      # 'from all images of digit i, keep only the ones written by the same writer'
      # CHANGE TO Y_PERSON OR NOT?
      pool <- pool[metadata$person_id[pool] == metadata$person_id[i]]# who wrote image i
      
    } else { # if not the same writer, pool must be diff writer + same digit (neg pair)
      
      pool <- pool[metadata$person_id[pool] != metadata$person_id[i]]
      
    }
    sample(setdiff(pool, i), 1) # doesn't allow pairing with itself
    
  }, integer(1)) # each iteration must return 1 integer
  
  cbind(a,b)
}
```
:::


From make_pairs() (which creates the two image indices; pair-index matrix), we 
must extract the actual images + the target y (0 if diff writer, 1 if same), 
using make_batch().


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_batch <- function(p, # pairs created by make_pairs()
                       images = x, # actual images
                       class_labels = y_person) { # class assoc with images
  
  y <- matrix(as.integer( # true = 1, false = 0
    class_labels[p[, 1]] # labels of first col of p-i matrix
                         == class_labels[p[, 2]]), # label of second col
              ncol = 1) # matrix of 1 col for formatting for neural network
  
  # return the actual images + the target
  list(
    left = images[p[, 1], , , , drop = FALSE], # left side of Siamese
    right = images[p[, 2], , , , drop = FALSE], # right side of Siamese
    y = y
  )
}
```
:::


Training/validation/test split has to be done by writer, so that we can test the
generalisability of the model by evaluating its performance on writers it truly 
hasn't seen before.
Limitation - only 20 writers.

We decided on a 60/30/10 split?



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# get the writer IDs belonging in each split
set.seed(25)
writers <- unique(data$metadata$person_id - 1L)
train_writers <- sample(writers, 0.6*length(writers))

rest_writers <- setdiff(writers, train_writers)
set.seed(25)
valid_writers <- sample(rest_writers, 0.75*length(rest_writers))
test_writers <- setdiff(rest_writers, valid_writers)

# now extract the image IDs belonging to each split
train_ids <- which(data$metadata$person_id %in% train_writers)
valid_ids <- which(data$metadata$person_id %in% valid_writers)
test_ids <- which(data$metadata$person_id %in% test_writers)

# now make the image index pairs in each split
train_pairs <- make_pairs(train_ids, length(train_ids), data$metadata)
valid_pairs <- make_pairs(valid_ids, length(valid_ids), data$metadata)
test_pairs <- make_pairs(test_ids, length(test_ids), data$metadata)

# for each pair, extract the image + 0/1
train <- make_batch(train_pairs)
valid <- make_batch(valid_pairs)
test  <- make_batch(test_pairs)
```
:::


Build the shared encoder:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
image <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1)) # each image = 28x28, 1 image channel

z <- image |>
  layer_conv_2d(16, 3, activation = "relu") |> # learns useful features (shapes, strokes)
  layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |> # makes feature maps smaller while keeping important info
  layer_conv_2d(32, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_global_average_pooling_2d() |> # converts feature maps -> single vector of numbers
  layer_dense(16) # converts to 16-no embedding representing the handwriting style

encoder <- keras_model(image, z)
# NOTHING HAS BEEN CHANGED FOR THE ABOVE FROM THE NOTES -- CHANGE IF WANTED
```
:::


Build the Siamese model:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# a & b = describes pair of images supplied to model
a <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
b <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

# encoders produce the embeddings for a & b
# distance calculates the Euclidean distance between their embeddings 
distance <- list(encoder(a), encoder(b)) |>
  layer_lambda(f = function(z) {
    op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(z[[1]] - z[[2]]), 
                   axis = 2, # sum over embedding dimension
                   keepdims = TRUE) + 
              1e-7) # makes sure it's not 0
  })

# distance = model output
model <- keras_model(list(a, b), distance)
```
:::


Choice of loss - contrastive loss. 
(Since this function works with pairs of images, which is how our data is already 
organised, this is a natural/simple choice for evaluating pairwise whether the 
digit was computed by the same or different writer) -- change.

Loss func = 1 for same-writer pair, 0 for diff-writer pair.
("The loss makes same-writer images move closer together and different-writer images move at least 1 unit apart.")


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
contrastive_loss <- function(y, d) {
  op_mean( # finds avg loss across all pairs in a batch
    y * op_square(d) + # squares each pair's distance - for same-writer pairs, penalises a large distance
            (1 - y) * op_square(op_maximum(1 - d, 0))) # for diff writer pairs, penalises only if distance is < 1: if dist >=1, penalty is 0
}
```
:::


Compile model: (only train + validation data)

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model |> compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3),
  loss = contrastive_loss
)

model |> fit(
  list(train$left, train$right), train$y,
  validation_data = list(
    list(valid$left, valid$right), valid$y
  ),
  epochs = 5,
  batch_size = 64
)
```

Now we must select a threshold at which below = same and above = different.
To do this, we look at validation pairs and compute the accuracy "for actual same pairs and actual different pairs, then average those two rates. The balanced accuracy metric gives both kinds of pair equal weight." [notes]


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_distance <- as.numeric(predict(model, list(valid$left, valid$right)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_same <- as.logical(valid$y[, 1])

balanced_accuracy_at <- function(cut) {
  predicts_same <- valid_distance < cut
  same_rate <- mean(predicts_same[valid_same])
  different_rate <- mean(!predicts_same[!valid_same])
  (same_rate + different_rate) / 2
}

example_thresholds <- unique(as.numeric(
  quantile(valid_distance, c(.25, .5, .75))
))
data.frame(
  threshold = example_thresholds,
  balanced_accuracy = vapply(example_thresholds, balanced_accuracy_at, numeric(1))
)
```
